title: Is Mayonnaise Dairy? What Is Actually in Mayo

seo.title: Is Mayonnaise Dairy? Ingredients Explained
seo.meta_description: Traditional mayonnaise is made from oil, egg, and an acid such as vinegar or lemon—not milk. Commercial sauces can vary, so labels still matter.
seo.search_intent: Determine whether mayonnaise contains dairy and what to check for lactose or milk allergy.

excerpt: Traditional mayonnaise is not dairy. It is an emulsion of oil, egg yolk, and an acidic ingredient such as vinegar or lemon juice. Egg and milk are separate allergens.
content_html:
Traditional mayonnaise is not a dairy product. Its basic structure combines vegetable oil, egg—usually yolk—and an acidic ingredient such as vinegar or lemon juice. Milk, cream, and butter are not required to make mayonnaise.

The confusion comes largely from appearance. Mayo is pale, thick, and creamy, and many other creamy sauces do contain dairy. Mayonnaise gets that texture from an emulsion: tiny droplets of oil stay dispersed in a water-based phase with help from compounds in egg yolk.

Classic mayonnaise is built from oil, egg, and acid

The U.S. standard of identity for mayonnaise defines it as an emulsified semisolid food prepared from vegetable oils, acidifying ingredients such as vinegar or citrus juice, and one or more egg-yolk-containing ingredients. Salt, spices, and certain other optional ingredients are allowed.

Milk is not required. Homemade mayonnaise follows the same principle: oil, yolk, acid, and salt are enough to create a stable sauce. Its color can range from ivory to yellow depending on the eggs and oil.

Calling mayo dairy because it looks creamy therefore confuses texture with origin. Cream is creamy because it contains milk fat; mayonnaise is creamy because oil and water have been emulsified.

Egg matters for allergy, but egg and milk are different allergens

Conventional mayonnaise usually contains egg and is therefore unsuitable for someone with an egg allergy unless a specific egg-free version is used. Food-labeling systems treat egg and milk separately because they contain different allergenic proteins.

A person with milk allergy still should not assume every mayonnaise-based product is safe just because classic mayo is dairy-free. Flavored products, ranch-style dressings, cheese sauces, “creamy” spreads, and restaurant mixtures can add milk, whey, cheese, or cream.

The ingredient list is more important than the color or texture. Plain mayonnaise is commonly milk-free; a sauce that happens to contain mayonnaise may have a completely different formula.

Standard mayo does not need lactose either

Lactose is the sugar found in milk. A mayonnaise made only from oil, egg, acid, and seasonings has no dairy ingredient supplying lactose. For someone with lactose intolerance, plain mayo is generally a different category from cream- or cheese-based sauce.

Brands still vary, so check the label if you need strict lactose avoidance, especially with gourmet flavors, prepared dressings, and food-service products whose recipes are less visible.

It is also important not to confuse lactose-free with milk-free. Dairy ingredients can have lactose removed while still containing milk proteins, which matters for milk allergy even when lactose intolerance is not an issue.

Vegan mayo changes the emulsifier, not the dairy definition

Vegan alternatives replace egg yolk with ingredients such as plant proteins, starches, or aquafaba. They are typically made without egg and dairy, although the actual label remains the authority.

Vegan mayo is not “more dairy-free” because regular mayonnaise was secretly dairy. Standard mayonnaise was already usually milk-free; the major change is removal of egg and other animal-derived ingredients.

Depending on local labeling rules, egg-free products may use a different legal product name rather than simply “mayonnaise,” but the shopper's practical question is still what the ingredient list contains.

Mayonnaise-based sauces are where the confusion becomes real

Burger sauce, tartar sauce, spicy mayo, coleslaw dressing, commercial aioli, and flavored spreads may all start with mayonnaise and then add other ingredients. Some remain dairy-free; others do not. A cheese-mayo sauce obviously introduces milk even though the original mayo base did not contain it.

At restaurants, ask about the complete sauce instead of stopping at the word mayo. With a severe allergy, cross-contact from utensils and shared containers can matter as well.

Packaged sandwiches, deli salads, and ready-made dips are another reason to read the full ingredient statement. A tuna salad can use dairy-free mayonnaise but add cheese; a potato salad can include sour cream; a bottled “aioli” can be formulated with milk solids even when the restaurant-style version you know is not. For milk allergy, the safest shortcut is not to classify the dish by texture or by the word mayo, but to check the declared milk allergen for that exact product and ask about preparation when the food is sold without a label.

The general answer remains dependable: traditional mayonnaise is an oil-and-egg emulsion, not a dairy food. Creamy appearance does not prove milk is present; the specific product label tells you whether dairy was added.

faq.question: Does mayonnaise contain milk?
faq.answer: Traditional mayonnaise does not require milk; it uses oil, egg, and an acid such as vinegar or lemon. Some flavored sauces and commercial variants can add dairy ingredients.

faq.question: Does mayonnaise contain lactose?
faq.answer: Basic mayonnaise without dairy ingredients has no source of lactose. Check flavored products and restaurant sauces if strict avoidance is necessary.

faq.question: Is mayonnaise safe for egg allergy?
faq.answer: Conventional mayonnaise usually contains egg and is not suitable for someone with egg allergy. Egg-free alternatives are available.
